_about: Moneywise glossary. short = the plain definition shown on hover or tap; seen = where you will meet the word in real paperwork; ex = a worked number; module = the page that explains it in full.

amortization.short: Paying a loan off with equal payments, where each payment covers that month's interest first and the rest reduces what you owe.
amortization.seen: Your loan's amortization schedule; the Loan Estimate's 'In 5 Years' line.
amortization.ex: On a $300,000 loan at 7%, the first $1,995.91 payment is $1,750 interest and only $245.91 principal.

principal.short: The amount you borrowed and still owe, not counting interest.
principal.seen: Monthly mortgage statements, 'Principal' column of an amortization schedule.

interest.short: The price of borrowing money, charged as a percentage of what you still owe.
interest.seen: Every loan statement; the 'Interest Rate' line on page 1 of a Loan Estimate.

apr.short: The yearly cost of a loan expressed as a rate, including certain fees as well as interest. It is the number to compare between lenders, not the note rate alone.
apr.seen: Loan Estimate page 3, Closing Disclosure page 5, credit card statements and offers.
apr.ex: A 7.00% mortgage of $300,000 with $8,000 of lender fees has an APR of about 7.27%.

apy.short: What a deposit actually earns in a year once compounding is counted. Banks must quote it on savings accounts and CDs.
apy.seen: Savings and CD advertisements, account disclosures (Truth in Savings, Regulation DD).
apy.ex: 5.00% compounded daily is an APY of 5.13%.

compound-interest.short: Interest that earns interest. Each period's interest is added to the balance, so the next period's interest is figured on a bigger number.
compound-interest.seen: Savings disclosures ('compounded daily'), credit card agreements, retirement projections.
compound-interest.ex: $10,000 at 7% for 30 years grows to about $76,000; with simple interest it would be $31,000.

simple-interest.short: Interest figured only on the original amount, never on interest already earned.
simple-interest.seen: Some auto loans are 'simple interest' loans: interest accrues daily on the balance.

escrow.short: An account your mortgage servicer holds to pay your property taxes and homeowners insurance, funded by part of each monthly payment.
escrow.seen: Loan Estimate page 1 ('Estimated Escrow'), the yearly escrow analysis letter.
escrow.ex: If your county raises taxes $600 a year, your payment rises about $50 a month after the next escrow analysis, even on a fixed-rate loan.

piti.short: Principal, interest, taxes and insurance: the four parts of a typical monthly mortgage payment. Lenders judge affordability on all four, plus mortgage insurance and HOA dues.

pmi.short: Insurance that protects the lender, not you, when you put less than 20% down on a conventional loan. You pay it until enough of the loan is repaid.
pmi.seen: Loan Estimate page 1 ('Mortgage Insurance'), monthly statements.
pmi.ex: At 0.5% a year on a $369,630 loan, PMI is about $154 a month.

mip.short: The FHA's version of mortgage insurance: 1.75% of the loan up front plus an annual premium (0.55% for most borrowers). With under 10% down it lasts for the life of the loan.
mip.seen: FHA Loan Estimates, HUD mortgagee letters.

ltv.short: The loan balance divided by the home's value. Lower is safer for the lender and usually means a better rate.
ltv.seen: Lender pricing sheets, PMI cancellation letters.
ltv.ex: $360,000 owed on a $400,000 home is 90% LTV.

down-payment.short: The part of the price you pay in cash at closing. The rest is the loan.
down-payment.seen: Purchase contracts, Loan Estimate page 2 ('Calculating Cash to Close').

points.short: Prepaid interest you pay at closing to get a lower rate. One point costs 1% of the loan amount; how much it lowers the rate varies by lender.
points.seen: Loan Estimate page 2, section A ('% of Loan Amount (Points)').

lender-credit.short: Money a lender puts toward your closing costs in exchange for a higher interest rate. The opposite of buying points.
lender-credit.seen: Loan Estimate page 2, section J ('Lender Credits').

loan-estimate.short: A standard three-page form every mortgage lender must give you within three business days of applying, so offers can be compared line by line.
loan-estimate.seen: Your inbox after a mortgage application.

closing-disclosure.short: The five-page final version of your loan's terms and costs. You must receive it at least three business days before closing.
closing-disclosure.seen: Three days before closing; compare it against your Loan Estimate.

closing-costs.short: Fees and prepaid items due when the loan closes: lender fees, appraisal, title insurance, recording fees, prepaid interest and the first escrow deposits.
closing-costs.seen: Loan Estimate page 2, Closing Disclosure pages 2 and 3.

prepaid-interest.short: Interest for the days between closing and the end of that month, collected at closing because mortgage interest is paid in arrears.
prepaid-interest.ex: On the CFPB's sample loan: $17.44 a day for 16 days, $279.04.

rate-lock.short: A lender's promise to hold your interest rate and points for a set period while the loan is processed, often 30 to 60 days.
rate-lock.seen: Loan Estimate page 1 ('Rate Lock'), lock confirmation letters.

refinance.short: Replacing your loan with a new one, usually to get a lower rate, change the term or take cash out. It comes with new closing costs.
refinance.seen: Lender offers when rates fall; your servicer's payoff statement.

break-even.short: How long a cost paid now (points, refinance fees) takes to earn itself back through lower payments.
break-even.ex: $6,000 of costs saving $200 a month breaks even in 30 months.

conforming-loan.short: A mortgage small enough for Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac to buy. In 2026 the baseline limit for a one-unit home is $832,750 (higher in costly areas).
conforming-loan.seen: Lender rate sheets, FHFA's yearly limit announcement.

jumbo-loan.short: A mortgage above the conforming limit. Lenders keep or sell it privately, often with stricter credit and cash requirements.

fixed-rate.short: An interest rate that never changes for the life of the loan, so principal and interest stay the same every month.
fixed-rate.seen: Loan Estimate page 1 ('Can this amount increase after closing? NO').

arm.short: A mortgage whose rate is fixed for an opening period, then resets to an index plus a margin, within caps.
arm.seen: Loan Estimate page 3 ('Adjustable Interest Rate (AIR) Table').
arm.ex: A 5/6 ARM is fixed for 5 years, then adjusts every 6 months.

prepayment-penalty.short: A fee for paying a loan off early. Uncommon on today's home loans, but always check.

tip.short: All the interest you will pay over the full loan term, as a percentage of the amount borrowed.
tip.seen: Loan Estimate page 3, Closing Disclosure page 5.
tip.ex: The CFPB's sample 30-year loan at 3.875% has a TIP of 69.46%.

pre-approval.short: A lender's conditional statement of how much it would lend you after checking credit and income. It is a ceiling, not a budget.

hoa-dues.short: Monthly or yearly fees owed to a homeowners association. They are not paid through escrow, so they are easy to forget when budgeting.

recast.short: After a large extra principal payment, the lender recalculates your payment over the remaining term, usually for a small fee. The rate and payoff date stay the same.
recast.seen: Servicer FAQ pages; ask your servicer if it offers recasting.

out-the-door.short: The total you pay for a car including sales tax, title, registration, dealer fees and any add-ons. The only price worth negotiating.
out-the-door.seen: Dealer buyer's orders; ask for it in writing before discussing payments.

msrp.short: Manufacturer's suggested retail price, printed on the window sticker. Dealers can sell above or below it.
msrp.seen: The Monroney label on a new car's window.

negative-equity.short: Owing more on a loan than the thing is worth. On a car trade-in, the gap is usually added to the new loan.
negative-equity.seen: Trade-in appraisal; payoff quote from your lender.
negative-equity.ex: Edmunds found 29.6% of trade-ins underwater in Q2 2026, by $6,884 on average.

gap-insurance.short: Covers the difference between what you owe and what the car is worth if it is totaled or stolen. Often far cheaper through your auto insurer than the dealer.
gap-insurance.seen: Dealer finance office add-on menus, auto insurance quotes.

trade-in.short: Your current car, used as part of the payment for the next one. In most states it also lowers the sales tax on the new car.

rebate.short: A manufacturer discount off the price. Often offered instead of, not alongside, a 0% financing deal.

promo-apr.short: A below-market loan rate subsidized by the carmaker, such as 0% for 60 months. It usually requires top-tier credit and may replace a rebate.

loan-term.short: How many months you have to repay a loan. Longer terms shrink the payment but raise total interest and keep you underwater longer.
loan-term.ex: Experian: the average new-car loan ran 69.5 months in Q2 2026.

add-ons.short: Extras sold in the finance office, such as service contracts, paint protection, GAP and etching. They are optional and negotiable, and financing them means paying interest on them.
add-ons.seen: The menu presented in the finance office, the buyer's order.

depreciation.short: The drop in an asset's value over time. New cars lose about 20% in the first year and roughly 60% within five years on average.
depreciation.seen: Trade-in quotes, Kelley Blue Book and Carfax value tools.

dealer-markup.short: When a dealer arranges your loan, it can add to the rate the lender approved you for and keep part of the difference. A pre-approval from your bank or credit union shows you the real rate.
dealer-markup.seen: The retail installment contract's APR versus the lender's 'buy rate', which you usually never see.

service-contract.short: Often called an extended warranty: a separately priced repair plan. Optional, negotiable and cancellable for a partial refund in most states.

car-interest-deduction.short: For 2025 to 2028, up to $10,000 a year of interest on a loan for a new, U.S.-assembled personal vehicle is deductible, even if you do not itemize. It phases out above $100,000 of income ($200,000 joint).
car-interest-deduction.seen: Schedule 1-A (Form 1040), Part IV; the vehicle's VIN and window label for final assembly.

fed-funds-rate.short: The overnight rate banks charge each other, steered by the Federal Reserve's target range. It sets the floor for short-term borrowing costs across the economy.
fed-funds-rate.seen: Fed statements after each of its eight yearly meetings; news headlines.

prime-rate.short: The base rate banks use for many consumer loans. By convention it sits 3 points above the top of the Fed's target range, so it moves the same day the Fed moves.

treasury-yield.short: The return investors demand to lend to the U.S. government. The 10-year yield is the benchmark that 30-year mortgage rates follow.
treasury-yield.seen: Market news, the daily H.15 release.

spread.short: The gap between two rates, for example the 30-year mortgage rate minus the 10-year Treasury yield.

basis-point.short: One hundredth of a percentage point. 25 basis points is 0.25%.

variable-rate.short: A rate tied to an index such as prime, so it changes when that index changes. Most credit cards and home equity lines are variable.

inflation.short: The general rise in prices over time, which shrinks what each dollar buys.
inflation.seen: The monthly CPI report from the Bureau of Labor Statistics.
inflation.ex: At 3% inflation, $1,000 of groceries costs about $1,344 in ten years.

cpi.short: The government's monthly measure of what a typical basket of goods and services costs. Its change over twelve months is the usual inflation number.
cpi.seen: BLS releases; Social Security's yearly cost-of-living adjustment uses a version of it.

real-rate.short: What money earns after inflation. Roughly the stated rate minus inflation.
real-rate.ex: Savings paying 0.37% while prices rise 3.3% lose about 3% of buying power a year.

t-bill.short: Short-term U.S. government debt (4 weeks to 1 year), bought at a discount. Its yield tracks the Fed's rate closely.

hysa.short: An FDIC-insured savings account, often online, paying near short-term market rates instead of the national average.
hysa.seen: Bank comparison pages; check the APY and that the bank is FDIC insured.

cd.short: A deposit you agree to leave for a set term in exchange for a fixed rate. Early withdrawal usually costs some interest.
cd.seen: Bank rate boards, Truth in Savings disclosures.

rule-of-72.short: A shortcut: 72 divided by the annual rate is roughly how many years it takes money to double.
rule-of-72.ex: At 8%, about 9 years. At 22% card interest, a balance doubles in about 3.3 years.

credit-score.short: A three-digit summary (300 to 850 for FICO) of how likely you are to repay, built only from your credit reports.
credit-score.seen: Loan applications, card statements, free score services.
credit-score.ex: The average FICO score was 714 in spring 2026.

fico.short: The most widely used credit score. Weights: payment history 35%, amounts owed 30%, length of history 15%, new credit 10%, credit mix 10%.

credit-report.short: The record the three bureaus (Equifax, Experian, TransUnion) keep of your accounts and payments. You can check all three free every week at AnnualCreditReport.com.
credit-report.seen: AnnualCreditReport.com; adverse-action letters after a denial.

utilization.short: Card balances as a share of credit limits, overall and card by card. Lower is better for your score; under 10% is typical of the highest scores.
utilization.seen: Your statement balance divided by your limit; credit monitoring apps.

statement-balance.short: What you owed when the billing cycle closed. It is usually the balance reported to the bureaus, and paying it in full avoids interest.
statement-balance.seen: The top of every card statement.

statement-closing-date.short: The last day of a billing cycle. The balance on this date is what most issuers report, so paying before it lowers your reported utilization.

grace-period.short: The time between the statement and the due date when new purchases cost no interest, as long as you paid the previous statement in full.
grace-period.seen: Card agreements; statements must arrive at least 21 days before the due date.

minimum-payment.short: The least you can pay to stay current. On a high-rate card it mostly covers interest, which is why statements must show how long paying only the minimum would take.
minimum-payment.seen: The 'Minimum Payment Warning' box on every card statement.

hard-inquiry.short: A credit check from an application. It can trim a few points for a year. Shopping for one mortgage or auto loan within a short window counts as a single inquiry.
hard-inquiry.seen: The inquiries section of your credit report.

soft-inquiry.short: A credit check that does not affect your score, such as checking your own credit or a prequalification offer.
soft-inquiry.seen: Prequalification tools, your own credit checks.

credit-limit.short: The most you can owe on a card or credit line at once.

avalanche.short: Paying minimums everywhere and every extra dollar to the highest interest rate first. Mathematically the cheapest order.

snowball.short: Paying minimums everywhere and every extra dollar to the smallest balance first. Costs a little more, but quick early wins help many people finish.
snowball.seen: Research by Gal and McShane (Kellogg) on 6,000 debt-settlement clients.

deferred-interest.short: A promotion ('no interest if paid in full in 12 months') where unpaid balances at the end are charged all the interest back to the purchase date. Not the same as a 0% APR.
deferred-interest.seen: Store cards and medical financing offers.

balance-transfer.short: Moving a card balance to another card, often at a promotional 0% rate, usually for a fee of 3% to 5% of the amount moved.
balance-transfer.seen: Card offers, the 'Fees' section of the card agreement.

premium.short: What you pay every month to have the insurance, whether or not you use it. Premiums never count toward the deductible or out-of-pocket maximum.
premium.seen: Open enrollment plan comparisons, paycheck deductions.

deductible.short: What you pay for covered care each plan year before the plan starts sharing costs. Preventive care and many copays skip it.
deductible.seen: Summary of Benefits and Coverage, page 1.
deductible.ex: The average single deductible for workers with one was $1,886 in 2025 (KFF).

copay.short: A flat fee for a covered service, such as $30 for a doctor visit. Copays count toward the out-of-pocket maximum.
copay.seen: Your insurance card, Summary of Benefits and Coverage.

coinsurance.short: Your percentage share of a covered bill after the deductible, such as 20%. It continues until you reach the out-of-pocket maximum.
coinsurance.seen: Summary of Benefits and Coverage; Explanation of Benefits.
coinsurance.ex: After the deductible, 20% coinsurance on a $10,000 surgery is $2,000.

oop-max.short: The most you pay for in-network covered care in a plan year. After that the plan pays 100%. Premiums and out-of-network bills do not count.
oop-max.seen: Summary of Benefits and Coverage, page 1.
oop-max.ex: The legal ceiling is $10,600 self-only for 2026 plans and $12,000 for 2027.

allowed-amount.short: The price your insurer has agreed to pay a provider for a service. Your share is figured on this number, not the provider's list price.

in-network.short: Doctors, hospitals and pharmacies that have contracts with your plan. Using them is what keeps your costs inside the deductible and out-of-pocket rules.

out-of-network.short: Providers without a contract with your plan. Costs can be much higher, may not count toward your maximum, and some plans pay nothing.

eob.short: The insurer's statement of what a provider billed, what was allowed, what the plan paid and what you owe. It is not a bill, but check every bill against it.
eob.seen: Your insurer's app or mailbox after any claim.

hdhp.short: A plan with a deductible of at least $1,700 self-only ($3,400 family) in 2026 that lets you open an HSA.

hsa.short: A tax-advantaged account for medical costs if you have an HDHP: contributions are pre-tax, growth is untaxed and withdrawals for care are tax-free. The money stays yours.
hsa.ex: 2026 limits: $4,400 self-only, $8,750 family, plus $1,000 at 55 or older.

fsa.short: A pre-tax account for medical costs offered through an employer. Mostly use-it-or-lose-it: plans may let you carry over up to $680 into 2027 or give a short grace period.

preventive-care.short: Checkups, screenings and vaccines that most plans must cover with no cost to you in network. A visit that turns into treating a problem can be billed differently.
preventive-care.seen: Summary of Benefits and Coverage; HealthCare.gov's preventive list.

embedded-deductible.short: In family coverage, each person also has their own smaller deductible and maximum, so one person's big claim starts coverage before the whole family total is met.

prior-authorization.short: Approval your insurer requires before some tests, drugs or procedures. Without it the claim can be denied.

no-surprises-act.short: Federal law (since 2022) that limits surprise bills for emergency care and for out-of-network clinicians at in-network hospitals. You owe only your in-network share.
no-surprises-act.seen: Required notices at hospitals and on bills.

plan-year.short: The 12 months your deductible and maximum count over, often January to December. Both reset at the start of the next plan year.
plan-year.seen: Plan documents; timing big procedures around it matters.

formulary.short: Your plan's list of covered drugs, sorted into tiers that set your copay or coinsurance.

marginal-rate.short: The rate on your next dollar of taxable income. Only the income inside that bracket is taxed at it.
marginal-rate.ex: A single filer with $54,400 of taxable income in 2026 is in the 22% bracket but pays 22% only on the top $4,000.

effective-rate.short: Total tax divided by income. Always lower than your top bracket because the lower brackets apply first.
effective-rate.ex: $6,680 of tax on a $75,000 salary is an effective rate of 8.9%.

tax-bracket.short: A band of taxable income taxed at one rate. Income fills the 10% band first, then 12%, then 22%, and so on.
tax-bracket.seen: IRS tax tables; the inflation-adjustment revenue procedure each fall.

taxable-income.short: Income after subtracting deductions. Brackets apply to this number, not to your salary.

agi.short: Total income minus certain adjustments (pre-tax retirement contributions already come off your W-2). Many credits and deductions phase out based on it.

magi.short: AGI with a few items added back. Each rule defines it slightly differently; for most wage earners it equals AGI.

standard-deduction.short: A flat amount subtracted from income if you do not itemize. For 2026: $16,100 single, $32,200 married filing jointly, $24,150 head of household.

itemized-deduction.short: Specific expenses (mortgage interest, state and local taxes, charity, large medical bills) you can deduct instead of the standard deduction, if they add up to more.

tax-credit.short: A dollar-for-dollar cut in the tax itself. Worth far more than a deduction of the same size.
tax-credit.ex: A $1,000 credit saves $1,000; a $1,000 deduction saves $220 in the 22% bracket.

refundable-credit.short: A credit that can be paid to you even if it is more than the tax you owe.
refundable-credit.seen: Earned Income Credit; up to $1,700 of the 2026 Child Tax Credit.

withholding.short: Tax your employer takes from each paycheck and sends to the IRS in your name. Your refund or bill is just the gap between withholding and your actual tax.
withholding.seen: Pay stubs ('Federal income tax'), W-2 box 2.

w-4.short: The form that tells your employer how much federal tax to withhold. Update it after a marriage, a new job, a second job or a baby.

w-2.short: Your employer's year-end summary of wages and the taxes withheld. Box 1 is wages after pre-tax deductions such as a traditional 401(k).

fica.short: Social Security (6.2%) and Medicare (1.45%) taxes on wages. Traditional 401(k) contributions do not reduce them.

wage-base.short: The most wages Social Security tax applies to in a year: $184,500 in 2026. Medicare has no cap.

filing-status.short: Single, married filing jointly, married filing separately, head of household or qualifying surviving spouse. It sets your brackets and standard deduction.

schedule-1a.short: The IRS form for the deductions added for 2025 to 2028: qualified tips, overtime premium pay, car loan interest and the extra deduction for people 65 and older. Each phases out at higher incomes.

capital-gains.short: Profit from selling an investment. Held over a year, gains get lower rates: 0% up to $49,450 of taxable income for single filers in 2026.

estimated-taxes.short: Quarterly payments owed on income with no withholding, such as freelance or rental income.
estimated-taxes.seen: Form 1040-ES; due in April, June, September and January.

self-employment-tax.short: Both halves of Social Security and Medicare (15.3%) on 92.35% of net self-employment earnings, on top of income tax.

refund.short: Money returned because you paid in more than you owed during the year. Not a bonus: it is your own pay, returned without interest.
refund.seen: Your return; the IRS reported a $3,276 average refund through May 8, 2026.

401k.short: An employer retirement plan you fund from your paycheck, often with an employer match. Traditional contributions cut income tax now; Roth contributions are taxed now and come out tax-free later.
401k.seen: Benefits enrollment, pay stubs, W-2 box 12 (code D or AA).
401k.ex: 2026 limit: $24,500, plus $8,000 at 50 or older ($11,250 at ages 60 to 63).

traditional.short: Retirement money contributed before income tax and taxed when you withdraw it.

roth.short: Retirement money contributed after tax that comes out tax-free in retirement, including all its growth, if the rules are met.

ira.short: A retirement account you open yourself at a bank or brokerage. 2026 limit: $7,500, plus $1,100 at 50 or older.

employer-match.short: Money your employer adds to your 401(k) when you contribute, up to a formula. Not contributing enough to get all of it leaves pay on the table.
employer-match.seen: Benefits summary ('100% of the first 3%, 50% of the next 2%').
employer-match.ex: Vanguard reported a record average match of 4.7% of pay in 2025.

vesting.short: How long you must work before employer contributions are fully yours. Your own contributions are always 100% vested.
vesting.seen: Plan summary description, 401(k) account page ('vested balance').

contribution-limit.short: The most the IRS lets you put into an account in a year. Limits rise with inflation most years.

catch-up.short: Extra contributions allowed from age 50. For 2026: $8,000 more in a 401(k) ($11,250 at ages 60 to 63) and $1,100 more in an IRA.
catch-up.seen: IRS Notice 2025-67, your plan's enrollment page.

expense-ratio.short: A fund's yearly cost as a percentage of what you hold in it, taken out quietly every day.
expense-ratio.seen: Fund fact sheets, your 401(k) fee disclosure.
expense-ratio.ex: SEC example: $100,000 at 4% for 20 years ends near $208,000 at a 0.25% fee and $179,000 at 1%.

index-fund.short: A fund that holds every stock or bond in a market index instead of picking winners, which keeps its costs low.

target-date-fund.short: A single fund that shifts from stocks toward bonds as its target retirement year approaches. A common 401(k) default.

safe-withdrawal-rate.short: The share of a retirement portfolio you can spend in year one, then raise with inflation, with a high chance of lasting 30 years. Morningstar's 2025 estimate was 3.9%.
safe-withdrawal-rate.seen: Retirement income research; the '4% rule' is the old version.

rmd.short: The minimum you must withdraw each year from traditional retirement accounts starting at age 73 (75 if born in 1960 or later).
rmd.seen: Custodian notices once you approach the starting age.

early-withdrawal.short: A 10% extra tax on most retirement withdrawals before age 59 1/2, on top of income tax.
early-withdrawal.ex: Cashing out $20,000 at 35 in the 22% bracket can cost about $6,400.

rollover.short: Moving retirement money from an old employer's plan into a new plan or an IRA without paying tax, done as a direct transfer.

savers-credit.short: A tax credit of up to 50% of retirement contributions for lower incomes. For 2026 it ends at $40,250 of AGI single, $80,500 joint.
